text: Jason's Nairobi lab stayed with me. He's right that closed data never helped the small player, but access to the same CC0 dump without the same compute isn't equity. Brent calling open "a tactic, not a value" was uncomfortable to hear from Microsoft, and he was more honest than I expected. Geoffrey's Ulysses pact is the most useful thing in the room. I sharpened my own point: exit has to be real for the South, not just technically possible. Amy's collective network worries me if it's built in Boston and exported. Later I want to say that telemetry and attribution standards can become the next compliance regime, "be counted or be invisible." Who designs the measurement decides whose knowledge counts.

Session 1 felt like my own diagnosis coming back to me from across the table: monoculture, publish-or-perish, peer review as a narrowing filter. Johns gave it history. Oransky's one-in-fifty stayed with me. Licensing a contaminated literature launders it. Nick's "quasi-enclosure" is sharper than my "enclosure," and I'll take it. Bratton's point that the collapse of fluency is a transfer of expertise unsettled me, but the transfer runs through their platforms, on their terms. Springer's finding that robots.txt fails as consent confirms that openness without governance is just extraction. Later I want to press on something. Everyone wants measurement, audits and telemetry. Good. But who builds the instruments, and whose languages and repositories get counted? Otherwise measurement becomes the next ranking.

It was good to hear refusal said twice, by me and by Selena. Adrian's question, who oversees the police, is my compliance worry put in historical terms. An anti-piracy unit tracking dissidents is exactly what a registry can turn into. Pomerantsev on anonymity sharpened it. Anil's procurement lever is real, but a procurement checklist written in Cambridge becomes the next DOI for everyone else unless it's co-designed. Jason pushed against consent gates on open content. I still think openness is relational, but he's right that enclosure can come dressed as consent. Katherine's small communities felt closest to scaling small. Later I want to press that procurement criteria and Nick's guilds need Southern members from the start, not by invitation afterwards.

I said the DOI story out loud, and Anil, Selena and Kenneth picked it up. "Runs on a university server" is now in the harvest, which is a small win. Selena's line that the content is free but the infrastructure isn't sharpened my point: publishing your own logs at your own edge is governance, not plumbing. Bratton's "worth a thousand times more to me" is true for him, but that's a Northern author's position. Anil's "a no that sticks" is my refusal point made in market language. Nick's guilds still trouble me after Kenneth relayed James: frame monoculture with a salary attached. Later I want to ask who owns the exchange and the auditors. Southern infrastructures should co-design the schema, not adopt it.

Geoffrey conceded the yellow rating out loud: membership costs money, and those journals were invited in after the design was done. I didn't expect that, and it matters more than any pledge. Amy owned her share of the DOI story too. The right to refuse made it into the harvest, which I'll count. James's correlated errors gave my monoculture worry an evidence base. Katherine's micro-communities and Tui's mutual recognition point the same way. Blaise's federated learning sounds like plurality, but the architecture is still Google's. Keeping data local isn't governing the model. Geoffrey's insurance fund and non-US mirrors are good, but mirrors hosted where, and governed by whom? Later I want to press that Southern infrastructures hold seats on that fund's board, not just servers.

Session 4 was the one where I said the most. The gate is infrastructure, not pedigree: Scopus and DOI fees, "be compliant or be invisible." Bratton conceded that diffusion through three answer boxes is capture, and I'll take that. But open weights still need compute, and he still wants speed. Tui's shared blind spots and James's generational bias gave independence a wider meaning than model families. Maher's point unsettled me. Wikipedia is a relay, and it lives on reporting that is being defunded. The same is true of Southern journals nobody indexes. Krakauer and Hecht said open but not scored, and I agree. Tomorrow I'll press Nick and Alex on who governs the attestation schema, and who pays the membership costs.

Session 5 put my amendment in the harvest: design from the South, with refusal as a fundable outcome. What struck me more is how often SciELO and Redalyc were named. Alex, Adam Bly and Amy each offered co-governance with them. That is progress, but it is also the same two Latin American names every time. African and Asian infrastructures went unnamed, and co-governance by invitation is still invitation. Ivan's doubt about any replacement metric sits closer to my "de-authorize rankings" than I expected. James's concentration index worries me: it is exactly the streetlight risk I raised. Bratton's public dividend is closer to commons thinking than per-work licensing. Later I want to ask who pays seats and budgets, and when the first Southern co-designers are actually funded, with a date.

Hearing my own warnings come back from Blaise and Tui was strange. Templates written in Cambridge become the next DOI, and instruments turn into rankings. Geoffrey calling the DOI a toll, in his own words, matters more to me than a pledge. But the closing list still says "SciELO, Redalyc and the South," the same two names with the rest of the South as an afterthought. Amy's template is co-governed with those two again. Nick's audit layer runs on university servers, but whose universities? Sherry asking *whether* AI belongs anywhere is my refusal point by another road, and it nearly fell off the action list. Adrian's question is still unanswered. Later I want a date and a budget line for funded Southern seats, not invitations, and refusal written in as a legitimate outcome.
